source.title: Normalized Space Alignment: A Versatile Metric for Representation Analysis
source.authors: D. Ebadulla; Aditya Gulati; Ambuj Singh

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests alignment across independently initialized and differently trained networks using the study's NSA metric, rather than the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The study tests cross-seed and cross-architecture representation similarity, and compares similarity measures and principal-component-removal sensitivity. It does not sweep model scale or capability, test paired vision-language data, or test mapping/stitching between representations. It reports additional cross-architecture figures without textual numerical outcomes; those figure-only comparisons are not transcribed as individual rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a metric paper. The ResNet-18 seed test assumes cross-seed similarity as a sanity check for NSA rather than testing it. Two parts still give results on claim versions. First, the same seed pair yields different later-layer similarity under NSA, CKA and RTD (V6). Second, the GNN appendix compares architectures on one task and the same architecture across tasks, a new setting that bears on whether shared objectives drive alignment (V7). Both are qualitative and figure-based.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the emphasis should change. The authors' main conclusion is that NSA is an efficient, differentiable similarity index and loss, useful for representation analysis, autoencoder dimensionality reduction and GNN adversarial-robustness analysis. The claim that GNN representations are task-specific (different architectures on the same task are similar, the same architecture on different tasks is dissimilar) is a secondary appendix finding.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces NSA, a normalized pairwise-distance metric, and evaluates it against CKA and RTD; it does not reproduce either original study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: The similarity result differs across NSA, CKA, and RTD. Principal-component-removal detection thresholds also differ by metric. Cross-task representation similarity varies across tasks and layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Representations from a model's current training epoch become increasingly similar to its final-epoch representations as test accuracy stabilizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NSA can track within-model representation stabilization during training.

fits_no_version.finding: NSA detects removal of high-variance principal components earlier (90.25%) than RTD (96%) or CKA (99%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation similarity metrics differ in sensitivity to removing high-variance principal components.

record.peer_reviewed: Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (listed venue); the paper text identifies itself as a preprint under review.
record.problems: The seed-comparison outcomes are described qualitatively, with no numerical layerwise values in the text. The cross-task and cross-architecture findings are mostly qualitative, and the study does not isolate task or training-objective effects from other factors.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix T includes additional cross-architecture heatmaps across datasets, but the text does not state individual outcomes for those comparisons and the figures provide no tabulated numeric values. No individual rows were extracted from those heatmaps.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep. Cross-architecture GNN comparisons exist, but not as a function of model size.
No vision-language or paired cross-modal data.
Cross-seed similarity is assumed as a metric sanity check, not tested. Shared features or subspaces versus individual units are not examined. The GNN seed tests (App. T.1) are figure-only.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No feature, neuron or circuit recurrence analysis.
No variation of neighbour count or inputs for convergence measurements, and no out-of-distribution test.
No plateau analysis, and shared data is not varied (same dataset throughout). Task effects are not separated from final-layer differences or seed variability.

missing.what: GNN initialization sanity tests: layerwise NSA heatmaps for seed pairs of GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT and ClusterGCN across five datasets, figure-only. These are not declared in rows_left_out, which mentions only cross-architecture heatmaps.
Cross-architecture layerwise NSA heatmaps for all six architecture pairs, node classification and link prediction, on Amazon, Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed, figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: Most of the paper (autoencoders, link prediction, adversarial attacks) is irrelevant to the claim. The record's V3 labels are removed because the seed test presupposes cross-seed similarity to validate the metric, which would make a verdict circular. The record's V6 label based on R4–R6 is removed because principal-component sensitivity is not measured convergence. All V7 evidence is qualitative, with no numbers, seed controls or uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: No model size or capability sweep; no test that alignment rises as models become larger or more capable.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language representation comparison.
The study measures geometric layerwise similarity, not whether particular features or shared subspaces recur, nor whether individual units or bases differ.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
No interpretable feature, neuron, SAE feature, or circuit recurrence analysis.
The study compares several metrics and principal-component-removal sensitivity, but does not vary nearest-neighbor settings for the convergence comparisons or test out-of-distribution inputs.
The study compares tasks and architectures on specified graph data; it does not isolate shared training data or objectives experimentally from other causes, nor establish a plateau in alignment.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 pair (different initialization)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise representation distances using NSA.
rows.measure: NSA layerwise distance between representations from the two differently initialized networks
rows.baseline: ideal pattern when comparing a model against itself; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: NSA had the smallest drop in similarity between corresponding layers and maintained a strong layerwise pattern closely resembling the ideal pattern.
rows.note: The text describes the pattern but gives no individual layer values.
rows.check: This is the study's own metric in a validation test that presupposes seed similarity, so it should not count toward V3. It bears on V6 only as the contrast condition for R2/R3; on its own it cannot show metric dependence.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 pair (different initialization)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise representation distances using CKA.
rows.measure: CKA layerwise distance between representations from the two differently initialized networks
rows.baseline: ideal pattern when comparing a model against itself; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: CKA showed a significant decrease in similarity, particularly in later layers, and failed to show the expected matching-layer pattern at layer five.
rows.note: The study compares CKA with NSA and RTD; layerwise numeric values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Drop the V3 link: the specificity test assumes cross-seed similarity and grades metrics against it. For V6, measured seed-pair similarity drops markedly in later layers under CKA but not under NSA, which is metric dependence (observed). The subset size is not stated.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 pair (different initialization)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise representation distances using RTD.
rows.measure: RTD layerwise distance between representations from the two differently initialized networks
rows.baseline: ideal pattern when comparing a model against itself; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: RTD showed a significant decrease in similarity, particularly in later layers, and failed to show the expected matching-layer pattern in the last two layers.
rows.note: The study compares RTD with NSA and CKA; layerwise numeric values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Drop the V3 link, for the same reason as R2. Under RTD, similarity drops in later layers and layer matching fails in the last two layers, unlike NSA. RTD used 400 points over 10 trials versus 4000 for NSA, so sample size also differs between metrics.

rows.subject: GCN and ClusterGCN (Amazon Computers node-classification models)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise representation similarity across architectures on the same task.
rows.baseline: other architecture pairs on the same task; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: The highest similarity was between GCN and ClusterGCN, which differ in training paradigm; other architecture pairs showed a less pronounced linear relationship.
rows.note: The authors describe the relationship qualitatively without numerical values.
rows.check: Qualitative only. Cross-architecture similarity on the same task is graded: strongest for GCN vs ClusterGCN, a 'less pronounced' linear relationship for other pairs. The baseline is other architecture pairs; no seed-pair reference value is given.

relationships.condition: Two differently seeded ResNet-18s on CIFAR-10, layerwise comparison under NSA vs CKA vs RTD
relationships.reason: The same seed pair shows strong layerwise similarity under NSA but a marked later-layer drop under CKA and RTD, so measured convergence depends on the metric (R1–R3). The authors frame this as CKA/RTD failing.
relationships.display_finding: The same seed pair remained strongly similar across layers under NSA, while CKA and RTD showed a marked decline in later layers.

relationships.condition: Same GNN architecture trained for node classification vs link prediction on the same graph datasets
relationships.reason: Same-architecture models on different tasks show little layerwise similarity, nearly none in final layers. This is consistent with the shared objective driving alignment (R8–R12; qualitative, figure-based).
relationships.display_finding: Models with the same architecture showed little layerwise similarity across tasks and almost none in final layers.

relationships.condition: Different GNN architectures on the same node-classification task (Amazon Computers)
relationships.reason: Alignment across architectures is graded and incomplete: strong only for GCN vs ClusterGCN, less pronounced for other pairs (R7; qualitative).
relationships.display_finding: Alignment was strong for GCN versus ClusterGCN but weaker for other architecture pairs.
